text: [excited] This is Max. And Max... just missed the bus. [short pause] Again. [chuckles] Not a problem though. Because as of this morning, Max is FIFTY times faster than you. [pause] [curious] Which raises a question. If Max is fifty times faster than you... why does his commute now take LONGER than yours? [mischievously] We did the maths. [short pause] It is so much worse than you think.

[excited] Okay, quick ground rules. Max's body gets the upgrade. Muscles, bones, tendons, reflexes. Everything moves fifty times faster, and it's tough enough not to rip itself apart doing it. [short pause] Everything else stays normal. His brain. His stomach. His skin. His weight. [pause] And the air around him. [mischievously] Keep an eye on that list, because every single thing on it is coming back for him. [excited] Oh, and stick around, because at some point in this video, Max jumps higher than the Eiffel Tower. [short pause] [sarcastic] Once.

[curious] So how fast is fifty times? [excited] A normal walk is about five kilometres an hour. Max's walk? Two hundred and fifty. A light jog, five hundred. That's faster than any passenger train running today. And a proper sprint... about twelve hundred and fifty kilometres an hour. [short pause] Now, the speed of sound is twelve hundred and thirty-five. [dramatically] So on paper, Max can sprint straight through the sound barrier. [pause] [mischievously] Hold on to that phrase, though. On paper.

[excited] But problems later. First, the good stuff! Washing up, normally fifteen minutes. Max? Eighteen seconds. The whole flat, hoovered in under a minute. A ten-minute shower takes him twelve seconds. [short pause] Well, the scrubbing does. The water still falls at normal speed, so mostly Max just stands there... waiting for it to land on him. [chuckles] He can type two thousand words a minute. Which sounds amazing, until you remember his brain didn't get the upgrade. So he types way faster than he can think, and every email is just... whatever was in his head at the time. [pause] [sarcastic] Max has had a strange week at work.

[excited] And then there are other people. Dave goes in for a high-five. A normal hand moves at maybe five metres a second. Max's hand? Two hundred and fifty. [short pause] [dramatically] At that speed, a high-five lands with about the energy of a heavy sniper round. [pause] That's why the upgrade matters. A normal hand would shatter. Max's hand is fine. [short pause] [sarcastic] Dave's hand has been better. [excited] So Max learns rule number one. Around people, move like you're carrying a full cup of tea. Always.

[curious] Now here's something real. In 2010, a team at Southern Methodist University put sprinters on a treadmill that measures every single push their feet make. They wanted to know what actually sets the human speed limit. [short pause] And it isn't how HARD your muscles push. It's how FAST. A sprinter's foot is on the ground for about a tenth of a second, and that's all the time you get to shove the planet backwards. Max's foot touches the ground for two thousandths of a second. No human muscle fires that fast, which is exactly the part we upgraded. [excited] So, problem solved! Max can sprint at twelve hundred and fifty... [pause] [sarcastic] No. No he can't.

[excited] Problem number one... grip. When you run, you push the ground backwards, and the ground pushes you forwards. But it can only push as hard as your shoes can grip. And grip depends on one thing. How heavy you are. [short pause] [sarcastic] Max didn't get heavier. [curious] So no matter how fast his legs go, his shoes can only shove him forward with about the force of a fifty-kilo bag of sand. Push any harder, and his feet just spin. [chuckles] Meanwhile, the faster he goes, the harder the air pushes back. And at about a hundred and seventy kilometres an hour, the air pushes back exactly as hard as his shoes can push forward. [dramatically] That's Max's REAL top speed. Fifty times faster legs... and he runs about four times faster than Usain Bolt. Nought to a hundred? About three and a half seconds. The same as a decent sports car. Not bad. [short pause] Not superhero. [mischievously] There is a cheat, though. More weight means more grip, and the air doesn't care what's in your bag. So if Max straps on his own body weight in tinned beans, his top speed jumps to about two hundred and forty. [laughs] The fastest Max will ever run... he's carrying seventy kilos of beans.

[excited] Problem number two... the air. Even at one-seventy, it's brutal. That's a Category Two hurricane blowing straight into his face, for as long as he's running. [curious] And this is the bit almost everyone gets wrong. Going twice as fast doesn't take twice the power to fight the air. It takes EIGHT times. Power goes up with the cube of your speed. [dramatically] So if Max somehow did hit twelve hundred and fifty, he'd need about ten megawatts just to shove the air out of the way. That's roughly what a high-speed train's motors put out. [short pause] [sarcastic] From one guy. In trainers. [excited] Even at his real top speed, he's putting out more power than a small car engine. And that power has to come from somewhere.

[excited] Problem number three... lunch. Muscles are only about a quarter efficient, so every bit of push costs Max four times as much in fuel. Running flat out, he burns about six hundred calories for every kilometre. His commute is five kilometres. [short pause] That's three thousand calories. About five Big Macs, before he's even sat down. [curious] And remember, his stomach didn't get the upgrade. It digests at normal speed. So even if he eats the Big Macs, they're not reaching his muscles any time soon. His muscles only carry about two thousand calories of quick fuel. At full speed, that's gone in about a minute. [pause] [mischievously] But luckily for Max... something else gets him long before that.

[dramatically] Problem number four. The one that actually kills him. Heat. Remember the quarter-efficient muscles? The other three quarters of that energy doesn't vanish. It turns into heat... inside Max. Running flat out, his body temperature climbs by about a third of a degree, every single second. [short pause] Ten seconds of running, and he's at forty-one degrees. That's a dangerous fever. Twenty seconds, and he's at the point where people die of heatstroke. [curious] And the human body can only dump about a kilowatt of heat by sweating. Nobody's body does better. So for every ten seconds Max runs... he has to lie down in the shade for about fifteen minutes to cool off. [excited] Which means his five-kilometre commute is ten little sprints, and about two and a half hours of lying on pavements. [pause] [sarcastic] Walking would take an hour. [short pause] So Max learns the most important rule of being fifty times faster. [chuckles] Mostly... don't be.

[excited] Problem number five. Brakes, corners... and his brain. Stopping comes down to grip again. The air helps a bit, but from top speed, Max still needs about a hundred metres to stop. Corners are worse. To turn at full speed without sliding, he needs a turning circle more than half a kilometre wide. [sarcastic] He can't turn onto his own street. He overshoots the whole block. [curious] And then there's his brain. Normal speed. It takes a person about a quarter of a second to react to something they see. At top speed, Max covers twelve metres in that time. Completely blind. Add his hundred metres of braking, and he needs to spot trouble more than a football pitch away. [pause] [sarcastic] Max isn't a superhero. He's a missile with anxiety.

[mischievously] But here's the thing. Grip only limits how hard Max can push along the ground. [excited] His arms don't need grip. He throws a ball for the dog. A decent throw is about a hundred kilometres an hour. Max's? Roughly FOUR times the speed of sound. [short pause] At that speed, the air hitting the front of the ball heats up to nearly a thousand degrees. The felt starts to scorch before it's even left the park. [pause] [sarcastic] The dog has not got it back yet. [excited] And nothing limits how hard he can push DOWN. So Max can jump. Straight up. About two hundred and ninety metres. That's higher than the top deck of the Eiffel Tower! [short pause] [curious] That one jump burned six hundred calories, and pushed his temperature up by eight degrees. [sarcastic] He did it once.

[softly] Which is why, when it finally matters... Max doesn't run. He couldn't anyway. His grip gives him the acceleration of a sports car, and the car is already too close. So he spends a quarter of a second being useless while his brain catches up. Then he scoops the kid up, gently, like she's made of glass. [short pause] [dramatically] And he goes UP. [pause] [warmly] Not fast. Not far. Just a careful two-metre hop that she'll remember as a fun bounce. [softly] The driver never even saw them.

[curious] So, is being fifty times faster worth it? [excited] For chores, for emails... badly... and for catching your phone before it hits the floor? Absolutely. But for actually getting anywhere, the grip, the air, the food and the heat all point to the same answer. The fastest Max can keep going without cooking himself is about eighteen kilometres an hour. [short pause] The speed of a decent jogger. [warmly] Fifty times faster... and he's stuck at your pace. Because speed was never the hard part. Getting rid of the heat is.

[mischievously] But Max has one more problem. Twenty-three people reported sonic booms coming from the park this week. [short pause] [whispers] And somebody would like a word. [pause] [excited] So, what would YOU do with fifty times speed? Best answer in the comments goes into a future episode. And if you want to see what happens when somebody goes faster than Max... [short pause] a LOT faster... subscribe. We're working up to it.
